full_judgment:
2. It appears that one Chandpur Tea Co Limited, the opposite party No. 1, filed the instant suit on 30-1-1984, against the petitioner and the opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 and the predecessor-in-interest of the opposite party Nos. 4 to 9, praying for a decree for declaration of title in the suit land and also for recovery of its possession, contending, inter alia, that the opposite party No. 1 is the owner of the suit land on obtaining lease from the Government. The said suit land was also recorded in the name of the opposite party No. 1 during the last settlement and survey operations. During the war of liberation in 1971, the defendants forcibly took possession of the suit land which is by the side of the main C & B road, however, after liberation the management of the opposite party No. 1, took possession of the suit land in 1974 but again in 1975 the defendants went into the possession of the lands mentioned in second schedule and constructed temporary huts and structures thereon. The officials of the opposite party No. 1 from time to time asked the defendants to vacate the suit land but instead, they filed a suit being the Title Suit No. 217 of 1980 in the Fourth Court of Munsif, Habiganj, praying for a decree for permanent injunction. The said suit was renumbered as the Title Suit No. 122 of 1985, on being transferred to the Court of Assistant Judge, Chunarughat, Habiganj. In the meantime, they raised further tin sheds in the suit land, as such, the opposite party No. 1 was constrained to file the instant suit, praying for a decree for declaration of its title in the suit land and for recovery of khas possession with a further declaration that the defendants have no right, title and interest in the suit land but were trespassers. 

 13. It appears that Chandpur Tea Co Limited filed the present suit praying, inter alia, for a decree for recovery of khas possession of the suit land. The suit land is situated by the side of the main road which is under the super-vision of the C&B Deptt of the Government. The present suit was filed by opposite party No. 1 on 30-1-1984. Earlier the petitioner and others filed a suit for permanent injunction against the opposite party No. 1 being Title Suit No. 217 of 1980, praying for a decree for temporary injunction. The said suit was also transferred to be tried along with the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Chunarughat, Habiganj, and both the suits were heard and disposed of analogously by the same judgment. The trial Court framed the following issues in respect of the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984: 

 (v)	Is the plaintiff in the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984 entitled to the decree for recovery of khas possession and other reliefs as prayed for? 

 16. The learned Munsif on consideration of the evidence on record found that the defendant-petitioner could not prove his claim that they raised the huts and other structures on receipt of alleged verbal permission from Mr Bruce either from 1955 or since 1964 or 1967. He also found that in his suit being Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 the petitioner did not claim any title by adverse possession rather their claim that they are in the suit land on oral permission from one Mr Bruce. But the claim of settlement of any land in their favour was neither averred nor found. As such, the learned Assistant Judge found that the plaintiff in Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 or the defendant No. 2 in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, could not prove on evidence as to their claim of oral permission from the concerned authorities of the Chandpur Tea Estate Company Ltd on the basis of even oral permission from the said Opposite Party No. 1, as such, he found that the defendants in Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, were not in legal possession of the suit land. On those findings the learned Assistant Judge dismissed the Title Suit No. 122 of 1985 and decreed the Title Suit No. 40 of 1984, allowing recovery of khas possession of the suit land. 

 19. It is apparent that the suit land is situated by the side of the land of C & Broad of the Government, at the periphery of the lands of the opposite party No. 1, as such, taking advantage of the situation of the land being far away from the main lands of the opposite party company and being by the side of the main road, the petitioner and other defendants raised their huts and structures including the tin-sheds, from time to time, without any lawful authority. As such, they do not have any semblance of any title whatsoever. They do not claim any right, by adverse possession. Besides, even if they are in possession since 1971, the instant suit for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession, was within the period of limitation of 12 years under Article 142 of the Limitation Act, taking into consideration of the provisions of the Bangladesh (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1972 (President's Order No. 12 of 1972). In that view of the matter, I find no reason to disagree with the concurrent findings of facts arrived at by both the Courts below.
